groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
Most people divide their days between two settings: home, sometimes called the first place, and work or school, the second place. In the late 1980s, the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg argued that healthy communities also need third places: cafés, barbershops, public libraries, parks, and similar spots where people gather informally, simply because they enjoy the company.

Such places share several features. Nobody is obliged to be there, and nobody has to play host. Conversation is the main activity, and a visitor's job title or income counts for little; a student and a company director may share the same table. Prices are low, the doors stay open for long hours, and a group of regulars gives each place its character. Because visitors keep meeting people outside their own family and profession, third places spread news, build trust among neighbors, and help newcomers feel that they belong.

Many observers worry that these settings are disappearing. In suburbs built around the car, there is often nowhere to walk to, and chain stores are usually designed to move customers through quickly rather than to let them linger. Online forums offer a partial substitute, since they allow strangers to talk freely. Critics point out, however, that a screen cannot fully replace the chance meetings that happen when people share a physical space.

The human body is never truly alone. Trillions of bacteria inhabit the skin, the mouth, and above all the large intestine, forming a community that scientists call the microbiome. For much of the twentieth century, bacteria were regarded chiefly as agents of disease, to be eliminated wherever possible. That view has changed dramatically: most of the microbes we carry are harmless, and many are indispensable.

Gut bacteria perform tasks that human cells cannot. They break down plant fibers that our own enzymes cannot digest, releasing compounds that nourish the cells lining the intestine. They manufacture certain vitamins, including vitamin K. Simply by occupying space and consuming nutrients, they also leave little room for harmful species to gain a foothold. In early childhood, moreover, contact with these residents appears to teach the immune system to distinguish dangerous invaders from harmless ones.

This partnership can be disturbed. Antibiotics, although they save lives, do not discriminate between harmful bacteria and beneficial ones, and a course of treatment may reduce the diversity of the gut community for months. Researchers have linked low diversity to a range of conditions, yet they caution that such links do not prove that one causes the other. Whether an altered microbiome produces an illness or merely accompanies it remains, in many cases, an open question.

options: How Chinese shipbuilders designed larger ships

listening.script: Imagine you're the captain of a ship in the Mediterranean about a thousand years ago. How do you know which way you're heading? Well, by day you watch the coast and the sun, and at night you use the stars. That works fine until the sky clouds over. So what did captains do in winter, when it could be cloudy for weeks? Mostly, they stayed home. Ships sat in the harbor for months. Now, the magnetic compass changed that. It came from China, where people had known for centuries that a magnetic stone, left free to turn, always settles in the same direction. At first it was used on land, for things like laying out buildings, not for travel. But by the early eleven hundreds, Chinese sailors were using it at sea, and by the end of that century it shows up in European writings too. And here's what I want you to notice. The compass didn't make ships any faster or any bigger. What it gave sailors was confidence. They could hold a course under a gray sky, out of sight of land. So the sailing season grew longer, merchants could fit more voyages into a year, and trade expanded. Later, of course, the same little needle helped sailors cross whole oceans. But that's next week's story.

listening.script: OK, quick question. Would you rather pick a dessert from a menu of five or a menu of fifty? Most of us would say fifty. More choice is better, right? Well, let me tell you about a famous study published in the year two thousand. Two psychologists, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper, set up a tasting table in a grocery store. Sometimes the table had twenty-four kinds of jam. Sometimes it had only six. Now, the big display attracted more shoppers. People love to look. But when it came to actually buying, about thirty percent of the people who saw six jams bought a jar. With twenty-four jams? About three percent. So what's going on? One idea is that comparing takes effort, and when there's too much to compare, we give up and walk away. Another is regret. With twenty-three jams you didn't pick, it's easy to imagine that one of them was better. Now, I should be honest with you. Later studies haven't always found this effect. It seems to appear mainly when the options are hard to tell apart and you don't already know what you like. So I wouldn't say choice is bad. I'd say that past a certain point, adding options stops helping, and sometimes it gets in the way.

options: How air conditioning has changed life in cities

listening.script: If you've ever walked out of a city park on a summer evening and felt the air get warmer within a block or two, you've met today's topic in person. It's called the urban heat island effect: cities tend to be warmer than the countryside around them. It's hardly a new discovery, by the way. An amateur weather-watcher named Luke Howard measured it in London some two hundred years ago. So why does it happen? Partly it's the materials. Asphalt and dark roofs soak up sunlight all day, and then, crucially, they give that heat back after sunset. That's why the gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night, not at noon, which surprises people. Then there's what's missing. Plants cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves, so when you swap fields for pavement, you lose that free air conditioning. And tall buildings on narrow streets trap warmth that would otherwise escape to the sky. Finally, there's the heat we produce ourselves, from engines and, ironically, from air conditioners, which cool the inside of a building by dumping heat outside. So the hotter a city gets, the more it heats itself. What can planners do? Planting trees and using paler, more reflective surfaces both help. Neither is a miracle cure, but in a heat wave, even a degree or two matters.

options: How fossils form and why so few living things become one
Where scientists should search to find new fossils
How fossils of sea animals differ from those of land animals

answers: How fossils form and why so few living things become one
higher.explanation: The professor walks through the 'chain of unlikely things' a fossil needs and concludes that the fossil record is very incomplete.

listening.script: Let me start with a slightly depressing fact. Almost nothing that has ever lived became a fossil. When an animal dies, it's normally eaten, or it rots, or the weather breaks down its bones. For a fossil to form, a whole chain of unlikely things has to go right. First, the body needs to be buried quickly, say, by mud at the bottom of a lake or by sand in a riverbed. That keeps scavengers away and cuts off oxygen, which slows decay. Even then, the soft parts usually vanish. It's the hard parts, bones, teeth, and shells, that last. Next, over a very long time, water moving through the sediment carries dissolved minerals into the tiny spaces inside a bone. Bit by bit, the minerals fill those spaces and may replace the original material, until what's left is, in effect, a copy in stone. And we're not done. That stone has to survive millions of years underground, and then erosion has to bring it back to the surface just when somebody happens to walk by. Now, think about what that means for the evidence. Which creatures are we most likely to find? Those with hard parts that lived in or near water. A jellyfish, or a bird in a mountain forest, had far worse odds. So the fossil record isn't a photograph of past life. It's more like a guest list with most of the names missing.

questions.prompt: Write an email to Professor Marlowe. Write as much as you can and in complete sentences.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

Dear Professor Marlowe,

My name is Wen Zhou, and I am a second-year student in your Tuesday lecture. Last week you mentioned that your lab studies how people learn new words and that it sometimes accepts student volunteers. I would very much like to help.

I am interested in this research because I learned English as a teenager, and I have often wondered why some words stayed in my memory while others disappeared. I would love to see how such questions are tested.

Although I have not worked in a lab before, I earned an A in your statistics course last year and am comfortable with spreadsheets. I am also careful and reliable, and I am free on Monday and Thursday afternoons.

Could you tell me what I should do to be considered? I would be glad to send my transcript or to visit you during your office hours.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Wen Zhou

stages.title: Writing · Academic Discussion

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on labor economics. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Moreno
professor.post: This week we are examining how young people enter the job market. In many industries, students work as interns for several months without pay. Supporters say that unpaid internships give beginners experience and contacts that they could not get otherwise. Critics answer that only students with family money can afford to work for free, so these positions make inequality worse. What is your view? Should unpaid internships be allowed, or should employers be required to pay every intern? Why?

students.name: Paloma
students.post: I think unpaid internships should be allowed. A small organization, such as a local museum or a charity, often has no budget for extra staff. If the law forced it to pay, it would simply stop taking interns, and students would lose a chance to learn. Some experience without pay is better than no experience at all.

students.name: Gideon
students.post: I disagree. Unpaid positions are open only to people who can afford them. My cousin turned down an unpaid internship in another city because she could not cover the rent there. The student who took it was not more talented, just richer. That is not a fair way to start a career.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

In my opinion, unpaid internships should not be allowed, except for very short ones of a week or two. I agree with Gideon that they shut out talented students who cannot afford to work for free. Paloma is right that small organizations have little money, but I do not think free labor is the answer. Instead, universities or local governments could offer small grants so that museums and charities can pay their interns at least the minimum wage. I would also add a point that has not been mentioned: pay changes how interns are treated. When a company spends money on an intern, it has a reason to train that person properly and to give him or her meaningful tasks rather than a pile of photocopying. For these reasons, I believe paid internships are fairer for students and, in the end, more useful for employers as well.

groups.title: Take an Interview
groups.instructions: You have agreed to take part in a research study about learning new skills and hobbies. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

toefl.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about learning new skills and hobbies. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A skill I started learning last year is cooking. When I moved into a shared apartment for university, I realized that I could only make instant noodles and fried eggs. So I asked my mother to send me three simple family recipes, and I practiced one of them every weekend. At first the results were terrible. I burned the rice twice, and my roommates laughed at me. But I also watched short videos online to see the techniques, and little by little my food improved. Now I can cook about ten dishes, and I sometimes make dinner for the whole apartment. It has saved me a lot of money, too.

listening.script: Thank you for taking part today. Let's start with your own experience. Think about a skill or hobby that you started learning recently, or one that you learned in the past. What was it, and how did you go about learning it?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: For most things, teaching myself suits me better. The main reason is flexibility. With online videos, I can study late at night or early in the morning, and I can repeat a difficult part as many times as I need without feeling embarrassed. It is also much cheaper than paying for a course. However, I think it depends on the skill. When I tried to learn the guitar alone, I developed bad habits with my left hand, and nobody was there to correct me. So for physical skills like music or sports, I would choose a teacher, at least at the beginning. For everything else, I prefer to learn on my own.

listening.script: Thanks for sharing that. Some people like to learn a new skill by taking a class with a teacher, while others prefer to teach themselves with videos or books. Which way suits you better, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I partly disagree. It is true that children seem to pick up some things, such as the pronunciation of a foreign language, more easily than adults. They also have more free time and are not afraid of making mistakes. But adults have advantages of their own. They know how they learn best, they can plan their practice, and they usually choose a skill because they really want it, not because their parents decided for them. My father started swimming lessons at fifty, and after one year he could swim a kilometer. So I think the real obstacle for adults is not ability. It is a lack of time and the fear of looking foolish.

listening.script: Now I'd like to ask for your opinion. Some people say that it is much harder to learn a new skill as an adult than as a child. Do you agree or disagree? Why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Yes, I think employers should do this, at least for a few hours each month. First, a skill that looks unrelated today may become useful tomorrow. For example, an accountant who studies photography might later help with the company's website. Second, learning something new keeps people curious and reduces boredom, and workers who feel that their company invests in them are less likely to leave. Of course, there must be limits. A small business cannot let its employees study all week, and the worker should explain what he or she wants to learn. But within reasonable limits, I believe paid learning time benefits both the worker and the employer.

listening.script: Here is my final question. Do you think employers should give their workers paid time to learn new skills, even skills that are not directly connected to their jobs? Why or why not?
